title: 3 Aug 2026 (Madinah)
des: Saudi Prometric paediatrics recall, Madinah, 3 August 2026

questions.question: An infant has congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type with massive protein loss despite supportive care. What is the definitive treatment?
questions.exp: Finnish-type (NPHS1) congenital nephrotic syndrome does not respond to steroids or calcineurin inhibitors. Albumin, ACE inhibitor and indomethacin are used first, but definitive care is bilateral nephrectomy, dialysis and transplantation. The recall writer was unsure between ACE inhibitor and nephrectomy.
questions.d: Bilateral nephrectomy, dialysis, then renal transplant

questions.question: A child with thalassaemia on regular transfusions develops multiple ecchymoses and bruises 3 weeks after a transfusion. Bloods show low platelets, low WBC and low haemoglobin. What should you do?
questions.exp: New pancytopenia needs a bone marrow examination to look for marrow failure or infiltration. Electrophoresis and ferritin do not explain a fall in all three cell lines.

questions.question: A girl has multiple bruises and ecchymoses. Her father says he also bruises easily. Which inherited platelet disorder is most likely?
questions.exp: May-Hegglin anomaly is autosomal dominant (MYH9), so it passes from father to daughter, with giant platelets and Döhle-like inclusions. Bernard-Soulier and Glanzmann are recessive, and Wiskott-Aldrich is X-linked and affects boys.

questions.question: A child with dark skin pigmentation and a low blood count in all cell lines is suspected to have Fanconi anaemia. Which test confirms the bone marrow failure?
questions.exp: Pancytopenia with café-au-lait or dark pigmentation suggests Fanconi anaemia. Bone marrow biopsy confirms aplasia, and chromosomal breakage testing (DEB/MMC) confirms Fanconi anaemia.

questions.question: What is the most common predisposing factor for iron deficiency anaemia in infancy?
questions.exp: Preterm babies miss the third-trimester iron transfer and grow fast, so their iron stores run out early. They need iron supplements from a few weeks of age.

questions.question: A school-age child has nocturnal enuresis only, with no daytime symptoms. What is the most common underlying cause?
questions.exp: Primary nocturnal enuresis is linked to small functional bladder capacity, nocturnal polyuria (low night-time ADH) and high arousal threshold. Organic causes are uncommon.

questions.question: An infant has hyperammonaemia with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis and ketosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Hyperammonaemia with metabolic acidosis points to an organic acidaemia (propionic, methylmalonic). Urea cycle defects give hyperammonaemia with respiratory alkalosis and no acidosis. The recall wrote normal anion gap, but organic acidaemias cause a high anion gap.

questions.question: What is the most common complication of uncorrected tetralogy of Fallot?
questions.exp: Chronic cyanosis causes polycythaemia and hyperviscosity, so cerebral venous or arterial thrombosis is the most common serious complication. Brain abscess and endocarditis are less common.

questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease suddenly develops hemiplegia with weakness of the left side. What is the cause?
questions.exp: Sudden focal weakness in SCD is an ischaemic stroke until proven otherwise. Treat with urgent exchange transfusion.

questions.question: A child has a murmur with a widely split second heart sound. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Wide fixed splitting of S2 with a soft pulmonary flow murmur is typical of ASD.

questions.question: A child of short stature (height 115 cm) has a long scenario of an ejection systolic murmur. What is the cardiac lesion?
questions.exp: This recurring recall describes supravalvular aortic stenosis in a short child (Williams syndrome).

questions.question: An intravenous drug user develops fever, hepatomegaly and a new heart murmur. Which organism is most likely?
questions.exp: In IV drug users, Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of endocarditis, often of the tricuspid valve. Viridans streptococci are the most common cause overall in children with heart disease. The recall writer chose alpha-haemolytic strep.
questions.a: Alpha-haemolytic streptococcus on a normal valve

questions.question: A 6-week-old infant with transposition of the great arteries and a PDA has tachypnoea, cyanosis and cardiomegaly from heart failure. Which drug supports cardiac output?
questions.exp: Milrinone is an inodilator used for low-output heart failure. In a newborn with TGA who needs mixing, prostaglandin E1 keeps the duct open, but at 6 weeks with heart failure and a large duct, inotropic support is the recalled answer.

questions.question: A newborn has frothy secretions, drooling and hypoxia. The NG tube coils in the upper pouch on X-ray and there is no gas in the abdomen. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: A coiled tube with a gasless abdomen means no distal fistula, so it is pure oesophageal atresia. With a distal fistula, air reaches the stomach.
questions.a: Oesophageal atresia with distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula

questions.question: A child has fever, a rash and adopts a squatting position because of severe abdominal pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: This recurring recall (with a picture of a petechial rash spreading from the wrists and ankles) describes Rocky Mountain spotted fever, a rickettsial vasculitis. Treat with doxycycline at any age.

questions.question: Which condition is a contraindication to intraosseous access in that bone?
questions.exp: IO access is avoided in fractured bones, bones with osteogenesis imperfecta or osteopetrosis, and infected skin over the site.

questions.question: A child has fever, vesicles on the hands, feet and in the mouth, and diarrhoea. What is the management?
questions.exp: Vesicles on hands, feet and mouth are hand, foot and mouth disease (Coxsackie A16), which is self-limiting and needs supportive care (fluids, analgesia). Several recall writers chose acyclovir, which is only for herpes simplex or varicella.

questions.question: A child with scleroderma has Raynaud's phenomenon. What complication can occur?
questions.exp: Severe Raynaud's in systemic sclerosis can cause digital ulcers, gangrene and auto-amputation of the fingertips.

questions.question: What are airborne precautions?
questions.exp: Airborne infections (measles, varicella, TB) need an N95 respirator, a negative-pressure room and hand hygiene.

questions.question: A 2-week-old baby has greenish (bilious) vomiting and abdominal distension. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise and needs an urgent upper GI contrast study.

questions.question: A newborn has abdominal distension, delayed passage of meconium and a gush of stool on rectal examination. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Delayed meconium with an explosive gush after a rectal examination is classic Hirschsprung disease. Confirm with a rectal suction biopsy.

questions.question: A child has hepatomegaly, muffled heart sounds, congested neck veins and capillary refill over 2 seconds. What type of shock is this?
questions.exp: Muffled heart sounds with distended neck veins and hypotension (Beck triad) mean tamponade, an obstructive shock.

questions.question: A child with pneumonia deteriorates and has a tympanic percussion note on one side. What is the cause?
questions.exp: Hyper-resonance with reduced breath sounds means air in the pleural space. Dullness would suggest an effusion.

questions.question: A child has drooling, dyspnoea and fever. The lateral neck X-ray shows widening of the prevertebral soft tissue. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Widened prevertebral soft tissue on a lateral neck film is retropharyngeal abscess. Epiglottitis shows the thumb sign.

questions.question: A child with a retropharyngeal abscess has drooling and is in respiratory distress. What is the immediate airway management?
questions.exp: A threatened airway is secured by intubation (the recall keyed nasotracheal), followed by IV antibiotics and drainage. Intubation is done by the most experienced person, ideally in theatre.

questions.question: A cyst in the right hemithorax was seen on antenatal ultrasound (suspected CPAM/CCAM). The baby is born well. What is the next investigation?
questions.exp: Antenatally detected lung lesions need a postnatal CT chest (even if the X-ray is normal) to define the lesion and plan surgery.

questions.question: A child has failure to thrive and constipation. The picture shows a large protruding tongue. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Macroglossia, hypotonia, constipation, prolonged jaundice and poor growth suggest congenital hypothyroidism. Check TSH and free T4.

questions.question: A picture shows a midline swelling at the back of a newborn's head covered by skin, containing brain tissue. What is it?
questions.exp: An encephalocele is herniation of meninges and brain through a skull defect, usually occipital. Image with MRI before surgery.

questions.question: A picture shows an umbilical hernia in an infant. What will you tell the mother?
questions.exp: Umbilical hernias rarely strangulate and most close by 3-4 years. Refer if still present at 4-5 years or very large.
questions.d: It will strangulate in most cases

questions.question: A 13-year-old on dietary restriction still has high triglycerides and lipids. What is the next step?
questions.exp: When lifestyle measures fail in an adolescent with persistent dyslipidaemia, continue the diet and add drug therapy, usually a statin from about 10 years.
questions.b: Continue the diet and add a statin

questions.question: A boy has features of fragile X syndrome. Which investigation confirms it?
questions.exp: Fragile X is a triplet-repeat disorder, diagnosed by DNA (PCR and Southern blot) testing of FMR1, not by karyotype.

questions.question: A girl has short stature and a webbed neck. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: Turner syndrome (45,X) is confirmed by karyotype. Every short girl with no other cause should have one.

questions.question: How is Tourette syndrome diagnosed?
questions.exp: Tourette syndrome is a clinical diagnosis: several motor tics and at least one vocal tic for more than a year, starting before 18.

questions.question: A manager advises a doctor to act in the way that gives the best outcome for most patients. Which ethical theory is this?
questions.exp: Teleological (consequentialist) ethics judges an act by its outcome. Deontology judges it by duty and rules.

questions.question: An infant with a history of HIE and perinatal asphyxia has clusters of sudden extension of the neck and trunk. EEG shows slow irregular waves. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Clusters of flexor or extensor spasms with hypsarrhythmia (chaotic high-voltage slow waves and spikes) are infantile spasms, common after HIE.

questions.question: A CT brain picture shows a ring-enhancing lesion (brain abscess). What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Empirical treatment for a brain abscess is a third-generation cephalosporin plus metronidazole, adding vancomycin for staphylococci, with neurosurgical drainage if large.

questions.question: A girl cannot comb her hair and has proximal muscle weakness. What is the first investigation?
questions.exp: Proximal weakness with Gottron papules and heliotrope rash is juvenile dermatomyositis. CK is the first test.

questions.question: A child has ascending paralysis that has reached the abdomen (Guillain-Barré syndrome). What is the treatment?
questions.exp: IVIG (or plasma exchange) is the treatment for GBS with progressive weakness. Steroids do not help.

questions.question: Cryoprecipitate is rich in which factor?
questions.exp: Cryoprecipitate contains fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor and factor XIII.

questions.question: A boy's father is 178 cm and his mother is 155 cm. What is his expected adult height range?
questions.exp: Mid-parental height for a boy = (178 + 155 + 13)/2 = 173 cm, with a range of about ±7-8.5 cm, so about 166-180 cm.

questions.question: When is a large VSD with heart failure usually repaired?
questions.exp: Large VSDs causing heart failure or pulmonary hypertension are repaired in the first year (usually 3-12 months), before pulmonary vascular disease develops.
questions.b: Only if it fails to close by 10 years

questions.question: A child has abdominal pain and retching. The X-ray shows a foreign body at the pylorus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: A contrast study stopping at the pylorus with an object outline, and an NG tube that will not pass, fits an impacted foreign body. Several recalls describe this picture; gastric volvulus was the other option.

questions.question: A child has an obstructing foreign body at the pylorus. What is the management?
questions.exp: The recall answer was LLG (laparoscopy or laparotomy plus gastrostomy). An obstructing gastric outlet object that cannot be removed endoscopically needs surgical removal.

questions.question: A young child has episodes of rhythmic thigh rubbing with flushing, then is normal. What is the management?
questions.exp: Infantile masturbation (gratification) is benign and needs reassurance. It stops when the child is distracted.

questions.question: A 3-month-old has fever and a cough that got worse over 2 days. All the family have the same illness. What is the most likely organism?
questions.exp: Bronchiolitis in a young infant with sick family members is most often caused by RSV.

questions.question: A child has uncontrolled seizures and hypopigmented patches. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Ash-leaf macules with refractory epilepsy (often infantile spasms) suggest tuberous sclerosis.

questions.question: A child has fever, a rash, post-auricular lymph nodes and red eyes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Post-auricular and suboccipital lymphadenopathy with a mild rash that spreads from the face is rubella.

questions.question: A child with ALL has an infected central venous line. What is the empirical treatment?
questions.exp: Line infection in an immunocompromised child needs broad Gram-negative cover (piperacillin-tazobactam with an aminoglycoside) plus vancomycin for staphylococci.

questions.question: A negative Mantoux test in a child with TB is most likely due to what?
questions.exp: False-negative tuberculin tests occur with malnutrition, overwhelming TB, immunosuppression, HIV and recent live vaccines.

questions.question: A false-negative sweat chloride test can occur in which condition?
questions.exp: Oedema and hypoproteinaemia can give a false-negative sweat test. Adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism cause false positives.

questions.question: A child has fever, abdominal pain and a mass on CT abdomen next to the lumbar spine. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: A fluid collection in the psoas with fever, flank pain and a flexed hip is a psoas abscess, usually Staphylococcus aureus.

questions.question: An asthmatic child has an acute exacerbation. What do you give first?
questions.exp: A SABA (salbutamol) is the first treatment for an asthma attack, with oxygen and oral steroids.

questions.question: A child has intellectual disability, a musty odour of the urine and eczema. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Untreated PKU causes developmental delay, fair skin, eczema and a mousy (musty) odour.

questions.question: A child with stable SVT has a narrow-complex tachycardia. After vagal manoeuvres fail, what do you give?
questions.exp: In a haemodynamically stable child, give a rapid IV adenosine bolus. Cardioversion is for unstable SVT.

questions.question: A picture shows pustules and hyperpigmented macules in a newborn on day 1. What is the management?
questions.exp: Transient neonatal pustular melanosis is benign, more common in darker skin, and leaves macules that fade over weeks.

questions.question: A newborn has a soft scalp swelling that crosses the suture lines (picture). What is it?
questions.exp: Caput succedaneum is scalp oedema over the presenting part that crosses sutures and resolves in days. A cephalhaematoma is limited by sutures.

questions.question: A child on chemotherapy for maintenance had contact with varicella. What is the management?
questions.exp: A non-immune child on chemotherapy needs VZIG within 10 days of exposure (or prophylactic acyclovir), and chemotherapy is usually held.
questions.b: Hold chemotherapy and give varicella-zoster immunoglobulin

questions.question: A child has unilateral foul-smelling nasal discharge. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Unilateral, offensive, purulent nasal discharge in a toddler is a foreign body until proven otherwise.

questions.question: A child has a nasal polyp. What is the next investigation?
questions.exp: A nasal mass in an infant may be an encephalocele or glioma connected to the brain, so image with MRI before any biopsy. In an older child a polyp also needs a sweat test for CF.

questions.question: A CT picture shows mixed bony and membranous choanal atresia. What is the most common type?
questions.exp: About 70% of choanal atresia is mixed bony-membranous, 30% purely bony, and purely membranous is rare.

questions.question: A child with a bone-anchored hearing aid (BAHA) had a problem missed in the emergency department. What type of error was this?
questions.exp: The recurring BAHA scenario is keyed as a diagnostic error.

questions.question: A problem in a child with a bone-anchored hearing aid was missed in the emergency department. What should be followed to prevent it happening again?
questions.exp: Patient safety focuses on systems, policies and processes rather than blaming individuals.
questions.d: Follow a systematic (systems) approach to care

questions.question: A doctor interrupts a nurse rudely while she is working. Which principle does this violate?
questions.exp: Procedural justice means fair, respectful processes and treatment of colleagues. Recalls key disrespectful interruption as a breach of it.

questions.question: A newborn has respiratory distress and a scaphoid abdomen. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bowel in the chest leaves the abdomen scaphoid. Intubate (no bag-mask) and pass an NG tube.

questions.question: A diabetic child has a white coating on the tongue that wipes off (picture). What is this?
questions.exp: White plaques that wipe off to leave a red base are pseudomembranous candidiasis (thrush), common in diabetes.
